channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: New Legacy Fund website makes investments more accessible but transparency issue lingers
item.description: North Dakota Monitor: “North Dakota has launched a new website aiming to make Legacy Fund investments more transparent to the public. The long-awaited website allows users to see where and how the state has invested taxpayer money through the Legacy Fund, a sovereign wealth fund fueled by oil taxes, which is valued at $15 billion.”

item.title: Michelle Handelman’s 400-Item Digital Archive Makes Queer Cultural Memory Public
item.description: JSM Culture: “A screening flyer, a VHS cover mockup and a fundraising packet can hold as much history as a finished film. Together, those working materials show how an idea moved through a community, found an audience and survived the pressures around it. That wider record is now easier to enter through the Feminist Institute Digital Archive, where more than 400 items from filmmaker, visual artist and writer Michelle Handelman’s career have been gathered into a new capsule collection.”

item.title: Sixteen Colors
item.description: Found in my Calishat Snaps: “Sixteen Colors is an online archive for ANSI and ASCII artpacks. The artform was originally intended for display on computer textmode consoles. It gained popularity in the early nineties with the rise of dial-up Bulletin Board Systems (BBS).”

item.title: Yandex Suspends 2026 Guidance After Data Centers Come Under Fire
item.description: Moscow Times: “Yandex announced Thursday that it was withdrawing its 2026 financial guidance following a series of Ukrainian drone strikes against its data centers earlier this month, a move that triggered the tech giant’s stock to fall slightly in afternoon trading.”

item.title: Leaked DHS employee archive, Icepick, faces challenges to stay online
item.description: CyberScoop: “A company working on behalf of the Department of Homeland Security sought to cut off online access to information on more than 41,000 employees that hacktivists said they obtained from a database breached at DHS. A search tool for the database, named Icepick, went offline for a spell before coming online again Thursday under a different registrar.”

item.title: Meta settles with teen during trial testing claims social media caused depression, eating disorders
item.description: Reuters: “Meta Platforms has ​settled with a teen plaintiff who accused the company of designing Instagram and Facebook to be addictive, causing her mental ‌health problems and disordered eating, attorneys for the plaintiff said on Friday. The settlement came after jury selection began on Wednesday for a trial that was slated to test the claims of two teens, identified as S.J. and K.D.B., against Meta and Snapchat parent Snap Inc.”

item.title: How a six minute TikTok love story became a South African novel
item.description: The Citizen (South Africa): “It all began with a cellphone on her car dashboard and a six-minute fictional love story that millions of viewers fell in love with. It was a series on TikTok called Thato wa Ngwanyana, and it’s crossed over into the novel Good Things Keep Happening to Me.”

item.title: Bodycare builds 700-strong micro-influencer network
item.description: Retail Gazette: “The health and beauty retailer has partnered with PMC to develop AIMEE, a platform that analyses data on customers, stock, social media trends and store performance. The system is designed to help Bodycare make decisions on stock allocation, demand forecasting and local marketing, using insights from its network of micro- and nano-influencers.”

item.title: Belgian Finance Ministry hit by cyberattack, MyMinfin and other services offline
item.description: Brussels Times: “The digital services of the Belgian Ministry of Finance are currently affected by a cyberattack, making MyMinfin and several other services temporarily unavailable. However, there are no indications of a data breach or that any data has been compromised, the tax authorities announced on Wednesday.”

item.title: Influencer Indicted for Hunting White Shark off Wellfleet
item.description: Provincetown Independent: “Christopher Stefanou, 30, was arraigned on Oct. 21 after a Barnstable County grand jury returned indictments against him on charges of cruelty to animals and four Dept. of Marine Fisheries (DMF) regulatory violations for fishing for a great white shark off Marconi Beach under cover of darkness with a European customer a year ago. Stefanou, who has a sizable online following for his shark fishing, posted a dramatic 17-minute video on social media documenting the expedition.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: ‘Lord Farquuad’ addresses ‘massive’ 400-megawatt data center at city hall meeting
item.description: WKRC: “When addressing the gathering, ‘Lord Farquaad’ issued the following statement: ‘I would like to begin my comments today by advising the rest of this room to please put off their foul stench, it smells like too many poors, and too many working class in this room. And that is not the interest that we are interested in serving in my town of Duloc, and we should not be interested in serving those interests here in San Diego either. We should be interested in representing the business community, that represents the AI data centers, that represents the ability to monitor our constituents with our Flock cameras and we know these two things go hand in hand, of course.'”

item.title: Data center project proposed on federal land gets sent back to square one
item.description: Nevada Current: “Approval for the first-ever commercial data center on U.S. public lands was formally rejected on Thursday after a federal appeals board affirmed the Bureau of Land Management must conduct a separate environmental review, which in turn would have to be approved, before proceeding with the project.”

item.title: Texas officials huddled with tech companies before grid blitz
item.description: Politico: “Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has been cracking down on data centers for months, but less than a year ago his appointees and staffers were actively trying to bring projects to the state. On Dec. 16, 2025, two days before Texas announced sweeping changes to expedite grid access to data centers, Abbott’s top staff held a closed-door meeting with representatives of the state’s largest tech and transmission companies, according to records obtained by POLITICO.”

item.title: Zuckerberg Wants to Build a Giant Online Network of AI Agents
item.description: Gizmodo: “Meta’s goal of building a network of AI agents that work together to serve more than a billion people worldwide helps explain why the company isn’t ‘charging everyone up front’ to use Muse. The idea is to attract as many users as possible. It’s unclear exactly what this collaboration between agents will entail, but it raises questions about data sharing, an area where Meta has a checkered history.”

item.title: Amazon’s anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
item.description: CNBC: “Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to ‘tokenmaxxing’ in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools. The memo, which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company’s website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI.”

item.title: AI Street Cameras Tracking Parking Violations on the Upper West Side Taken Down
item.description: West Side Rag: “For the past six months, the curb management company, Automotus, monitored parking behavior on the Upper West Side using AI-powered cameras. The temporary installation of two of the company’s ‘CurbSight’ AI cameras along Broadway between West 74th and 75th streets ended this week, and the pilot’s results are now being analyzed by the New York City Department of Transportation.”

item.title: Washington’s message to AI execs: Please shut up
item.description: Axios: “Even pro-AI government officials and lawmakers wish AI founders would do what every other major industry chief does — shut up and just build their products … safely.”

item.title: Stanford removes all-white, all-male AI-generated depiction of marching band from website
item.description: Stanford Daily: “The Leland Stanford Junior University Marching Band (LSJUMB) is one of Stanford’s most photographed student organizations, having been featured on Stanford’s social media platforms and framed in campus buildings. But on Monday, members were shocked to find that Stanford had posted an AI-generated depiction of the group — all-white and all-male.”

item.title: Dartmouth provost resigns following accusations he used artificial intelligence for writing
item.description: Associated Press: “A top administrator at Dartmouth College has resigned after a faculty committee found he used artificial intelligence to shape his writing, including in a guest column in The Washington Post on AI cheating. The announcement Wednesday of Provost Santiago Schnell’s departure from the Ivy League university comes as colleges across the country grapple with how to transform teaching as more assignments can be completed with AI tools.”

item.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
item.description: TechCrunch: “Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year.”

item.title: How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites
item.description: Reuters: “Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere, home appliance ​company SharkNinja and engine manufacturer Cummins. Yet the hacker did almost none of the work.”

item.title: Owners of Elvis Presley’s Music Sue Anthropic for Copyright Infringement
item.description: New York Times: “The owners of Elvis Presley’s music sued the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, saying it trained its models on more than 200 of Presley’s songs without their permission, and accusing it of copyright infringement. The suit, filed on Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on behalf of several parties, seeks a jury trial and more than $41 million, or $150,000 per song, in damages.”

item.title: App’s AI “Eyes” for Blind Users Fall Short, UMD Researchers Find
item.description: University of Maryland: “A blind man points his phone at a pan and asks, ‘Are the sausages brown yet?’ The app he’s using responds out loud that some spots are still slightly pink. So a bit later, he takes another photo and asks again, and then again, about four times in all, until the food is fully cooked. What he really wanted, he later told researchers, was not a repetitive Q&A but useful advice: ‘Maybe it still looks pretty pink—stir a little more, maybe about five minutes.’ He was one of 11 participants, all of whom identify as blind, in a University of Maryland (UMD) study presented this year at a top human-computer interaction conference.”

item.title: How AI is transforming hurricane forecasts
item.description: NPR: “Hurricane forecasters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to make predictions — and they say the technology is rapidly transforming the field. When the first hurricane of the Atlantic season formed this month, an AI model beat out traditional models at predicting where it would go.”

item.title: Bear-vision: The AI-powered tech designed to reduce dangerous polar bear encounters
item.description: The Independent: “Artificial intelligence-powered ‘doorbell cameras’ are being trialled by an international team of specialists to alert local communities to approaching polar bears amid the growing threat of human conflict. Created by the conservation charity Polar Bears International, the initiative is part of a broader push to safeguard both human lives and wildlife as global warming escalates the frequency of hazardous interactions.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Independent Journalism Atlas
item.description: Spotted on Bluesky: From the About this project page: “The Independent Journalism Atlas is a wayfinder for an ecosystem most journalism coverage doesn’t cover — the thousands of independent creator-journalists building audiences, breaking news, and doing accountability work outside the institution. We’ve mapped 2,415 of them. We’re not done.”

item.title: CRTC launches new database to make it easier to identify Canadian music
item.description: Government of Canada: “The CRTC [Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission] is launching a free, downloadable music database that makes it easier for broadcasters, artists and the public to identify Canadian music. For the first time, information that broadcasters use to identify Canadian music is available in one place. The database brings together information previously spread across several industry sources, making it easier for Canadian artists to be discovered and played across the country.”

item.title: Exploring Bonnet House From Anywhere: Our Digital Collections Are Now Live
item.description: Bonnet House Museum & Gardens: “Through our new digital collections portal, we invite you to discover a wide variety of objects and materials from our holdings, offering a deeper look into the people, art, and history connected to the estate. At the present moment, you are able to explore the art of Frederic, Evelyn, as well as son Frederic Clay Bartlett, Jr. and daughter, Evie Lilly Lutz. Everything you see is housed right here at the museum, whether currently on display or carefully preserved in our climate-controlled storage.”

item.title: Meta loses appeals against interim measures imposed by French regulators
item.description: Reuters: “Meta Platforms has lost its appeals against interim measures imposed by French regulators over media organisations’ ​publishing rights in the Paris Court of Appeals, the court said ‌on Thursday.”

item.title: Roblox shares slump 17% as user growth and guidance miss expectations
item.description: Investing.com: “The gaming platform reported a loss per share of $0.32 for the third quarter, beating the analyst estimate of a $0.43 loss. Revenue reached $1.57 billion, surpassing the consensus estimate of $1.46 billion and marking a 16% increase year-over-year.”

item.title: Pinterest: Q3 Earnings Snapshot
item.description: Associated Press: “Pinterest Inc. (PINS) on Thursday reported third-quarter earnings of $21.5 million. On a per-share basis, the San Francisco-based company said it had net income of 4 cents. Earnings, adjusted for one-time gains and costs, came to 46 cents per share. The results fell short of Wall Street expectations.”

item.title: Only one person in the world can play this free Steam game at a time
item.description: TechSpot: “These days, a big online game is one that can drop 100 strangers onto the same map at once. Jono, a free platformer that quietly landed on Steam earlier this month, goes in the opposite direction entirely: there’s exactly one playable character for the whole planet, and everyone who downloads it has to wait in line for a turn.”

item.title: Binance Suspends Withdrawals After Crypto Hackers Steal $6.3 Billion
item.description: New York Times: “Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday that it had halted withdrawals after it was attacked by hackers who made off with more than $6 billion in digital coins, in what could be the biggest crypto heist in history.”

item.title: Utah files 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders, says the site breaks the state’s gambling laws
item.description: Salt Lake Tribune: “The state of Utah has filed 14 criminal charges, including 13 felony counts, against the prediction market site Kalshi and its co-founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, alleging the company has broken Utah law by promoting online gambling.”

item.title: Political information increasingly comes from pop culture, outside of partisan silos but where male creators – and sometimes misogyny – dominate
item.description: The Conversation: “Research on political polarization points to how people’s preferred news outlets and social media use create information silos, environments in which people primarily encounter views consistent with their own, further cementing those views. But this research often omits an important source of political information: popular culture, from influencers and podcasts to comedy, television and movies.”

item.title: New atlas of colorectal tumors sheds light on why cancers in young people are more dangerous
item.description: STAT News: “On Thursday, [Kimmie] Ng published a new study in Nature Medicine that may help illuminate critical differences between older and younger colorectal cancer patients. With 189 tumors, it’s the largest biological database — what researchers call a single cell atlas — of colorectal cancer tumors in patients ranging from their 20s to their 90s.”

item.title: Kew launches global seed platform to tackle native seed bottleneck holding back nature restoration
item.description: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew: “Today, the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (RBG Kew) launches the Seed Portal for Online Data (SeedPOD), a new open-access platform designed to tackle bottlenecks affecting global ecological restoration, by making native seed collections and the knowledge needed to grow them easier to discover.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Day 14 of NC Early Voting: So, So, So Close
item.description: Center for North Carolina Politics & Public Service at Catawba College: “Funded by a grant from the Z. Smith Reynolds Foundation and private donations to the N.C. Politics Center, [NC Elections Live] helps North Carolinians explore election results, compare voting patterns across election cycles, and better understand the state’s elections through publicly available data….the nonpartisan website draws its election data directly from publicly available files provided by the North Carolina State Board of Elections. The site is not affiliated with the State Board, county boards of elections, political parties, or campaigns.”

item.title: First Virtual Belarusian Jewish museum launches
item.description: Jewish News: “Before World War II, Belarus had a thriving Jewish population of an estimated 800,000 to 1 million people, making up around 14% to 15% of the total population, and more than 50% in cities like Minsk. An estimated 80% to 90% of Belarusian Jews (between 500,000 and 800,000 people) were murdered by Nazi Germany during the occupation between 1941 and 1943.”

item.title: Salford University to launch the Terry Eagleton Archive collection
item.description: About Manchester: “The University of Salford will launch a new archive collection from the internationally-celebrated literary scholar and cultural theorist Professor Terry Eagleton next month. Professor Eagleton, who was born in Salford, entrusted the collection to the University for its long-term preservation and research use. The extensive collection includes previously unseen manuscripts of his plays and poetry, cassette tapes, photos, handwritten notes and other material relating to his academic life, dating back from the early 1960s all the way to 2026.”

item.title: This map shows you which NYC restaurants are owned by private equity
item.description: FastCompany: “Via an interactive map of New York City, you can zoom in on any bar, restaurant, or café and learn whether it’s owned or backed by private equity or venture capital, and whether it’s public or privately owned.” Please note that “family ownership” can mean “owns a franchise of a restaurant chain.”

item.title: Meta silent after multiple Latino gay club social accounts felled
item.description: Bay Area Reporter: “Instagram and Facebook pages of two Latino LGBTQ clubs in Oakland were taken down last month. Despite the flurry of publicity surrounding alleged discrimination by Meta, Instagram’s parent company, spokespeople for the tech giant haven’t returned multiple requests for comment. The news comes as the issue continues to pop up for LGBTQ establishments nationwide. Anthem Orlando recently posted it had to make a new Instagram account.”

item.title: TikTok is going after Yelp and Google Maps with an in-app restaurant guide
item.description: The Verge: “The company on Wednesday announced the launch of Must Eat, a new section of the TikTok app built on 40 million posts, reviews, and comments about dining on the platform. The new feature uses videos and discussions of buzzy local businesses to create restaurant recommendation guides. Users can leave reviews of restaurants, call and make reservations, and search for nearby businesses on a map.”

item.title: Conservative influencers face identity theft charges over Minnesota primary
item.description: Minnesota Star Tribune: “The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office has charged conservative influencers Cam Higby and James O’Keefe with felony counts of identity theft and unlawful voting after they disguised themselves and attempted to vote during the state primaries in August.”

item.title: BBC unveils Global Signals research into the global information landscape to respond to the threat of disinformation
item.description: BBC: “The BBC World Service has launched Global Signals, groundbreaking new research to provide a deeper assessment of the online information space. The research will strengthen the BBC’s ability to understand and respond to disinformation and help build information resilience.”

item.title: Feed recommendations are the most common way teens encounter self-harm content
item.description: PsyPost: “An analysis of data from the 2025 OxWell Student Survey found that about a third of 11- to 18-year-old students in England had come across self-harm content online in the past month. Most of these encounters were unintentional, and about two-thirds of exposed students said the content had appeared in their social media feeds or been suggested while they were browsing. Students who were lonelier, had experienced other online harms, or had poorer mental health were more likely to report exposure. The paper was published in Nature Mental Health.”

item.title: DOOM Ported To A $30 Clamp Meter
item.description: Hackaday: “The clamp meter in question is the FNIRSI DMC-100, which can be had for the low price of just $30 or so if you know where to look. It’s a far cry from the many thousands of dollars you’d pay for a heavy old 486-based machine back in 1993. [Artur] got the doomgeneric engine running on the Artery AT32F415 chip that runs the clamp meter.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Mayor Mamdani Launches Online Resource to Help New Yorkers Keep SNAP and Medicaid Benefits
item.description: Government of New York City: “By answering a series of questions about their age, work status, education and other circumstances, users can learn whether they may be subject to the new requirements, qualify for an exemption or need to take additional steps to remain eligible. The site also connects New Yorkers with SNAP and Medicaid hotlines, food banks, job boards, approved volunteer opportunities and NYC Care. Those who have lost benefits or do not qualify for SNAP or Medicaid can find information about low- and no-cost health care through NYC Health + Hospitals’ NYC Care program and locate food assistance near them.”

item.title: Colorado’s Past Is Hiding in These 5,191 Old Newspapers
item.description: KOOL 107.9: “When the Palisade Tribune closed in 2014, several loose ends remained, including newspapers that represented more than a century of community history at risk of being forgotten. Palisade Historical Society to the rescue. PHS has preserved thousands of old Palisade Tribune newspapers by turning the pages into a searchable digital archive, and saving thousands of pages of Palisade, Colorado history.”

item.title: Google struggling to make AI Mode searches pay
item.description: The Register: “Shares in Google’s parent company Alphabet dived by almost ten percent on Wednesday, after the web giant admitted AI-powered searches earn it less money than it earns by serving ads with its old-school search engine.”

item.title: Reddit is the latest platform to embrace the ‘For You’ feed
item.description: TechCrunch: “Reddit is the latest social platform to adopt the “For You” feed popularized by TikTok. The company announced on Wednesday that users will now see two options when opening the platform: ‘For You’ and ‘Following.’ The ‘For You’ feed combines posts from communities users have joined with recommendations tailored to their interests.”

item.title: Meet the Gen Z Duo Who Left 60 Minutes and Launched Their Own Newsgirls Empire
item.description: Vanity Fair: “It’s easier to laugh off their naivete now that Newsgirls, their online news start-up aimed at Gen Z, has found an audience of nearly half a million followers across Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok. After bonding as the youngest hires at 60 Minutes—which marked each woman’s first gig out of college— [Mabel] Kabani and [Wren] Woodson launched Newsgirls in 2024 ‘to talk to people our age…[who] are just not watching traditional outlets anymore,’ Woodson tells Vanity Fair.”

item.title: Vox launches its first app with an eye toward building paid memberships
item.description: NiemanLab: “While the app is free to download and browse, it’s catered toward serving Vox journalism to paid subscribers in one place. Vertical videos and podcasts are free to watch and listen to, but only paid subscribers can read text stories and listen to podcasts ad-free.”

item.title: Top House Democrats demand Trump preserve conversations with Grok
item.description: Politico: “The top Democrats on the House Judiciary and Oversight Committees want President Donald Trump to preserve his conversations with artificial intelligence chatbots as part of an inquiry into whether Elon Musk’s AI assistant played a role in shaping White House policy — a preview of what’s to come if their party flips the chamber next week.”

item.title: Pentagon treating military base freezer malfunctions as suspected cyberattack, officials say
item.description: Reuters: “The Pentagon is treating the spate of mysterious freezer ​malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the United States in August as a suspected hack, according to four officials familiar with the matter. One of the ‌officials said the military investigators were in touch with their French counterparts about a similar cyberattack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets there earlier this month.”

item.title: Hackers Abuse Indian Government Domains to Push Illegal Gambling Websites Through Google Search
item.description: GBHackers: “Hackers have abused Indian government and educational domains to promote illegal gambling websites through Google Search, using unauthorized DNS changes to establish malicious subdomains while leaving legitimate websites operational.”

item.title: Haeinsa Temple Begins Recarving Tripitaka Koreana, a Project That May Take a Century
item.description: Seoul Economic Daily: “Haeinsa Temple in Hapcheon, Gyeongsangnam-do, held a ‘Daejanggyeong Woodblock Carving Gobulsik’ ceremony in the temple’s pagoda courtyard on the afternoon of the 29th, launching a long journey to newly carve all 81,352 woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana, a national treasure and UNESCO Memory of the World item. The Buddhist project is expected to take 50 to 100 years to complete. The people of Goryeo carved the Tripitaka Koreana over 16 years, from 1236 to 1251, when the country was in crisis from the Mongol invasions.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: MuGlobe.com
item.description: Came in over the transom: Per the email, the site “creates a virtual radio station from any spot on the planet and streams music for free, with no ads. It also has detailed articles about the music you’re listening to—its history, cultural context and how styles evolve over time—plus playlist support.” When you visit the site it takes you to a random place on the planet; I got dropped into the Congo Basin / Eastern Congo and was presented with a song called “Je m’en fous” in the form of a YouTube video. I confess to chairdancing.

item.title: Decoding WWII Training Aircraft Markings and Preserving John D. Voss’s Research
item.description: New-to-me, from Vintage Aviation News: “A few letters painted on the side of a WWII training aircraft can offer an important clue to its history. For John D. Voss, deciphering those markings became a research project that grew into USAAF Training Aircraft Fuselage Codes of WWII, a website dedicated to documenting the codes used by the United States Army Air Forces’ training schools.” Unfortunately the site does not have a security certificate, so expect a complaint from your browser.

item.title: Department of War Publishes Seventh Release of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Files on WAR.GOV/UFO
item.description: US DoD: “Today, the Department of War is publishing the seventh release of declassified and historical Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) files as part of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE). The collection continues to be housed on WAR.GOV/UFO, and the Department will release additional files on a rolling basis.”

item.title: Amazon just rebranded Kindle Unlimited — what you need to know about Kindle+
item.description: Mashable: “As of Oct. 22, Amazon rebranded Kindle Unlimited to Kindle+. Now under your subscription tab, you’ll find your membership listed as Kindle+. But what does this mean for your membership? Has the program or pricing changed? Here’s everything we know about Amazon’s rebrand from Kindle Unlimited to Kindle+.”

item.title: Microsoft offers a quarter of its global workforce voluntary buyouts as AI spending accelerates
item.description: Associated Press: “Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence. The company’s voluntary exit offer was available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States, the company’s Chief People Officer Amy Coleman wrote in a blog post Monday.”

item.title: Meta is charging government and nonprofit pages to post links on Facebook
item.description: Engadget: “[Daniel] Starks is one of a growing number of people to encounter Meta’s ongoing experiment with charging creators, businesses and other professionals to post links on Facebook. Meta says the test, which is part of its push to sell more subscriptions, isn’t supposed to affect pages for nonprofits or government entities. But that’s not the case, according to nonprofit leaders who spoke with Engadget.”

item.title: CNN’s Scott Jennings Hit With $72.5M Suit By Hasan Piker Over “Manipulated” Lynching Misquote
item.description: Deadline: “In a blistering response to Scott Jennings allegedly using ‘a false, fabricated, and manipulated video’ claiming Hasan Piker wants to bring back lynching of Black Americans, the left-wing streamer plans to take the CNN MAGA talking head to the courtroom cleaners for $72.5 million.”

item.title: Court orders Egyptian website closed in case seen as test for independent media
item.description: Reuters: “An Egyptian court convicted the editor-in-chief of leading independent news website Mada Masr ‌of running it without a licence on Tuesday, ordered the site closed and held her in custody for five hours, her lawyers and the outlet said. Lina Attalah of the online newspaper Mada Masr, which has won numerous international awards for its reporting, was fined 3 million Egyptian pounds ($53,400), her lawyers told Reuters. She was released ​after Mada Masr paid the fine, the newspaper said.”

item.title: Harnessing the power of the tides
item.description: UC Berkeley: “To combat climate change, countries worldwide are increasingly turning to clean energy sources such as solar and wind power in place of fossil fuels. Now, civil and environmental engineering professor Evan Variano is exploring another option: tidal energy. Using an underwater kite, he is studying ways to harness the power of ocean currents.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Brown student maps the hidden global labor powering AI
item.description: Discovered thanks to MottG on Mastodon. Brown University: “As part of an ongoing project to explore the material underpinnings of the digital world, [Cunyan Ma] has created an interactive map linking technology companies and their intermediaries to data workers around the world. The map, which is freely available online, aggregates existing data worker databases, Ma’s own data collection and news reports describing the conditions many data workers experience.”

item.title: Introducing MisophoniaResearch.com: An open space for misophonia research and collaboration
item.description: Shaylynn Hayes-Raymond: “MisophoniaResearch.com aims to make misophonia research easier to find, understand, and contribute to. The site brings together a research database, a directory of researchers and organizations, and space for discussion and collaboration. Participation is open to everyone with an interest in misophonia research, regardless of institutional or organizational affiliation. Researchers, clinicians, students, people living with misophonia, and other contributors are welcome.”

item.title: First-Ever Digital 3D Model of the Historic Stonewall Inn Launches
item.description: NYC LGBTQ Historic Sites Project: “LGBTQ preservationists and historians at the NYC LGBTQ Historic Sites Project and Making Gay History have launched the first-ever digital 3D model of the historic Stonewall Inn, including the surrounding Stonewall National Monument.”

item.title: Discord is making its public communities more searchable, and people have concerns
item.description: TechCrunch: “Starting November 16, every Discoverable Server will have its own web page, which may feature automated summaries of discussions in active public channels. Beginning in mid-December, selected messages from public channels may also appear in search engine results.”

item.title: Elon Musk’s AI-Generated ‘Odyssey’ Is Here to Save Western Civilization
item.description: Gizmodo: “So is it a good film? Well, no. It’s not a good film in the slightest. If anything, it reads more like a trailer or the overlong intro to a video game, the kind you skip halfway through the first viewing and then install a mod so you don’t have to smash the space bar every time.”

item.title: Yandex moves all three of its supercomputers to new site after Ukrainian drone attacks
item.description: Meduza: “Yandex has moved all three of its supercomputers — Lyapunov, Galushkin, and Chervonenkis — to new locations, its press service said. The supercomputers were not damaged during the Ukrainian drone attacks, Yandex said.”

item.title: Can This ‘Titan’ of TikTok Get Gen Z to Start Cooking?
item.description: New York Times: “Until 2023, no one had ever been honored with the title ‘queen of the mac and cheese subreddit.’ Then the chef and influencer Tini Younger posted her multistep, hyper-cheesy recipe on TikTok. Calling for six different dairy products and corkscrew-shaped pasta, it became an instant classic on many Thanksgiving tables — and ignited an annual debate that flared up again this month. That viral recipe also introduced Ms. Younger to an audience beyond TikTok, where she has built her career as one of the foremost food voices of Generation Z.”

item.title: A cybersecurity issue forces a major New Mexico hospital to divert patients and close clinics
item.description: Associated Press: “A major hospital network in New Mexico raced to fix a cybersecurity issue on Monday that forced it to send ambulances to other hospitals and left the state without an emergency department capable of treating the most serious injuries. The University of New Mexico Health System told people not to show up at its main hospital in Albuquerque and canceled appointments at its more than 30 clinics.”

item.title: Korea fines Google and Apple $47.6 million over in-app payments
item.description: Korea JoongAng Daily: “Korea’s media regulator fined Google and Apple a combined 63.71 billion won ($47.6 million) for forcing app developers to use their own in-app payment systems, three years after the companies were first notified of the proposed sanctions.”

item.title: Australia’s National Film and Sound Archive has rediscovered a lost 1926 silent film
item.description: ScreenHub: “Australia’s National Film and Sound Archive has announced the re-discovery of The Little Irish Girl, a silent film from 1926 starring Dolores Costello (the grandmother of actress and talk show host Drew Barrymore), which has been considered lost since the late 1940s.”

item.title: ‘It’s offensively cheap’: How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear
item.description: BBC: “The world’s solar power is crossing a threshold. A decade ago, it barely registered on a global scale, providing just 1% of the world’s power. In 2026, it will almost certainly increase to 10% of power, and overtake nuclear, a mainstay of electricity since the late 1970s.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: AI-written Disney guidebooks send tourists to rides that don’t exist
item.description: Boing Boing: “An underground monorail, non-existent bizarrely skinny killer whales, directions to extinct attractions, guide maps that bear no resemblance to reality. AI-generated Disney theme park guide books are flooding the market, filled with hallucinated slop that would drive a trusting tourist insane with misinformation.”

item.title: Facing pushback on data centers, tech giants are promising hosts more money and fewer secrets
item.description: Associated Press: “With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses.”

item.title: ‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre
item.description: The Guardian: “Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland. Now they are all gone. After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches.”

item.title: Major Data Center Developer Rents Floating Prison Barge to House Contract Construction Workers
item.description: Futurism: “According to Bloomberg, the boat is a three-story prison barge — a dull, gray rectangular ship that was once used as a floating detention center for migrants. It seems that Nscale will soon begin using the Kalmar’s 500 cots to house its new army of contractors, who will commute off the hulking barge to the jobsite.”

item.title: Editor’s note: AI is changing how City & State’s journalists work
item.description: City & State New York: “Well before the New York City Council’s marathon hearing on artificial intelligence safety this month, City & State had been on the front lines of AI, with award-winning reporting on the technology. And state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez writes in this week’s magazine about the need for further AI regulation in Albany. The technology is fundamentally changing how we gather and verify the information we publish.”

item.title: $137 Million in A.I.-Generated Ads Flood the Midterms
item.description: New York Times: “The ad, which included no disclaimer that it was A.I.-made, was one of more than 220 videos identified by the Wesleyan Media Project, a research group based at Wesleyan University, that used A.I.-generated fakery in ways large and small this midterm season — part of a wave of videos powered by artificial intelligence that have flooded the internet and television screens.”

item.title: Dan Sullivan promoted data centers in Alaska while his family business profits off them
item.description: Alaska Current: “Alaska Republican US Rep. Nick Begich III may be the state’s head data center cheerleader, but Republican US Sen. Dan Sullivan hasn’t been far behind. For years, Sullivan has echoed conservative Alaska lawmakers’ pitch that the state is the ideal location for a massive build-out of data centers needed to fuel the ongoing development of artificial intelligence software. And it just so happens that the proliferation of data centers is good business for the Sullivan family chemical company.”

item.title: Silicon Valley AI political groups turn on each other in the 2026 election
item.description: CNBC: “With one week until the midterm election, political groups favoring faster AI development and lighter, more uniform rules have spent roughly $8 million in general-election congressional races, besting groups pushing for stronger safeguards and more room for states to regulate that have spent about $6.9 million, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings through Oct. 20.”

item.title: WSU baseball removes AI-generated graphic after backlash
item.description: The Daily Evergreen: “WSU baseball posted a graphic to their social media Monday promoting their Cougar World Series, an intersquad tournament pitting the Cougs against each other. That post has since been removed. Why? Because it was generated with AI.”

item.title: UNC Chapel Hill offers new AI minor to all majors cross-campus
item.description: Spectrum Local News: “The new 15-credit-hour minor is part of UNC’s School of Data and Information Sciences, but it’s not just for computer science students. Students from fields including political science, psychology, nursing, business, biology and physics are already taking AI-related courses. The curriculum covers everything from using AI for writing, research and data analysis to understanding its limitations, reliability, safety and ethics.”

item.title: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
item.description: TechCrunch: “The latest use case for AI? Dumbing down your smart TV to get rid of the bloat. A number of developers and vibe coders have recently been sharing solutions for ‘vibe-coding’ your TV to get rid of sponsored ads, speed up the app launcher, redesign the home screen, disable tracking features, and more.”

item.title: Spotify Purged Over 50 Million AI Slop and Spam Songs From User Recommendations
item.description: Gizmodo: “Spotify’s ongoing war against AI slop has now targeted tens of millions of tracks. The music streaming giant announced Tuesday that it has removed more than 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from users’ recommendations so far this year. That’s on top of the more than 75 million spammy tracks the company says it has removed completely from its platform for serious or repeated violations of its rules.”

item.title: OpenAI, Meta caution US judiciary about risk of ‘deepfake’ evidence
item.description: Reuters: “Tech experts at OpenAI and Meta Platforms warned a federal judicial panel on Thursday that AI-generated ‘deepfakes’ are becoming so sophisticated that it will become increasingly challenging to determine the authenticity of audio and video evidence presented at trial.”

item.title: AI Search Tools Cited A Made-Up Concept Within A Week, Paper Finds
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok, and Google AI each cited posts about a made-up concept within seven days of the posts going up, according to a paper from researchers at Fudan University. The researchers published the posts from ordinary accounts on nine sites the tested tools already cited often. On two other topics, an opinion question with existing discussion and a made-up product, the same four tools picked up little in the same seven days.”

item.title: The Wall Street Journal’s new AI tool, “Doppler,” forecasts the issues that will shape the midterm elections
item.description: NiemanLab: “Rather than using AI-generated summaries to generate leads or help beat reporters monitor online content more efficiently, the Journal uses Doppler to conduct large-scale AI analyses quickly — and publishes those insights for readers. So far, analyses produced by Doppler have led to four major midterms stories in the Journal, with more expected to run before Election Day.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Launch of Valerio Adami online general catalogue
item.description: e-flux: “The Valerio Adami Archive announces the launch of work on the online general catalogue of Valerio Adami’s oeuvre. The project, promoted by the Archive and entrusted to the scientific direction of Lorenzo Madaro, is dedicated in this first phase to works created between 1958 and 1978, with the goal of being completed by December 2027.”

item.title: The Polish Museum of America is now in Minecraft!
item.description: Polish Museum of America: “We’re excited to announce that the Polish Museum of America (PMA) has officially joined the virtual world of Polonika in Minecraft! As one of the leading institutions dedicated to preserving and sharing the history, culture, and heritage of Polish Americans, we’re delighted to see our Museum brought to life in an entirely new and interactive way! Thanks to this exciting initiative by POLONIKA, players from around the world can now explore the Polish Museum of America virtually, discovering Polish cultural heritage through creativity, exploration, and play.”

item.title: Protests in Europe: Fact-checking viral videos amid claims of ‘chaos’
item.description: France24: “As young people protest poor school conditions and the rising cost of living across Europe, misleading videos are spreading online. Footage from Poland in 2017, military preparations in Portugal and a protest in Argentina have all been falsely presented as recent demonstrations in Europe, painting a misleading picture of unrest. Vedika Bahl fact-checks three viral videos to uncover what they really show and how old footage is recycled to spread misinformation and attract clicks.”

item.title: How Oakland rapper Bambu DePistola built his own music platform — literally
item.description: The Oaklandside: “The Filipino American emcee launched his new album ‘Bass Building’ through a custom streaming app on Oct. 1. It’s a daring play to advance worker’s rights in hip-hop.”

item.title: ‘Maxxing’ is Dictionary.com’s word of the year: ‘It’s cooler than saying you’re doing more’
item.description: The Guardian: “While ‘maxxing’ has been around in various forms for decades, it’s the phenomenon of ‘looksmaxxing’ – putting your physical appearance above all other concerns, and going to extreme lengths to improve it – that has fueled the recent rise in the word’s use.”

item.title: Consistency is key: A YouTube Shorts bonus program rewards creators who upload at regular intervals
item.description: Tubefilter: “YouTube is preparing to raise the entry threshold for its Partner Program, but at the same time, it is testing new ways for creators to make money. The platform quietly announced the launch of a Bonus Program that will deliver additional earnings to select Partner Program enrollees who consistently upload short-form content.”

item.title: Password, Please: Border Searches of Laptops, Phones Up 32% This Year
item.description: Gizmodo: “a new report… shows searches of the laptops and smartphones of visitors entering the United States have gone up 32 percent this year, according to data CBC News obtained from U.S. Customs and Border Protection. And this is with only the first three quarters of the 2026 fiscal year accounted for, which runs from Oct. 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026.”

item.title: Alleged Israeli spy company heavily targeted Starlink users, sources say
item.description: Reuters: “Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of ​Starlink’s satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.”

item.title: The open records stonewalling is working
item.description: CollegeJournalism.org: “Legal experts frequently discuss the idea that government actions can have a chilling effect on free speech, where the public self-censors to avoid potential government retribution. Abuse of the public records process likewise has a chilling effect on the public’s right to know. By creating procedural and financial hurdles, government actors aim to create enough delay and hassle that requesters give up. And they exhaust the journalists who are trying to answer questions these officials would rather not see asked at all. In an era where public trust in government and higher education is so low, both must prioritize transparency.”

item.title: New project mapping UK Continental Shelf provides boost to offshore infrastructure and development
item.description: British Geological Survey: “BGS is leading a new joint-industry project on behalf of The Crown Estate to develop a new suite of national-scale seabed geology and shallow subsurface datasets that will provide essential information across multiple marine sectors, including offshore renewables, linear assets and environmental management.”

item.title: Researchers create new database to track origins of water from space
item.description: Rice University: “All water comes from somewhere. Researchers who want to know where it comes from rely on water isotopes, variants of water molecules with slightly different masses, as location identifiers. In particular, the specific fraction of heavy to light water isotopes is unique to the water’s origin and processes it has undergone and can provide information on how water travels across the globe. From 2002 to the present, eight different satellite missions have been measuring the isotopes of water vapor around the planet, creating a rich dataset of water’s origins and movements.”

item.title: How a duck is putting a town ‘back on the map’
item.description: BBC: “The quacking idea was the brainchild of conservation architect Christian Montez, who has been donning a duck mask to highlight the history of his hometown of Leominster, Herefordshire. As well as featuring himself in his unusual attire, the videos include catchy songs played along to images of some of the town’s historical architecture.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: News from Special Collections & Archives: New Finding Aids Site is Live!
item.description: ZSR Library, Wake Forest University: “With our new site, we are proud to have incorporated some new features that we hope will make for a more efficient and enjoyable researching experience, providing access to to the 2,000+ archival collections stewarded by Z. Smith Reynolds Library Special Collections & Archives.”

item.title: Introducing PixelMeter: The Reviews Aggregator for Cameras, Lenses, Smartphones, and More
item.description: PetaPixel: “PetaPixel has announced PixelMeter, the camera industry’s first review aggregator platform. PixelMeter collects reviews from across the landscape and condenses the opinions into a single, standardized score so photographers can see the best gear at a glance.”

item.title: YouTube is reworking the Home page with Custom Feeds and quicker access to Subscriptions
item.description: DigitalTrends: “YouTube is changing how its Home page works, giving viewers more control over what shows up there and making some of the app’s most-used sections easier to reach. Custom Feeds are now replacing the existing topic chips for eligible users, while YouTube is also testing a redesigned top bar on mobile that moves Subscriptions closer to the Home feed.”

item.title: YouTube now gets twice as much watch time on U.S. TVs as any other platform
item.description: Tubefilter: “…in the August 2026 edition of The Gauge, YouTube had an especially strong showing. It claimed its biggest watch time share ever — 15.8% — as streaming platforms accounted for nearly half of the TV screen traffic recorded by Nielsen.”

item.title: ‘I’m 96 and have 15 million followers’: The grannies taking over TikTok
item.description: BBC: “Ninety-six-year-old Lillian Droniak, known as Grandma Droniak to her social media followers, went viral in June after claiming her retirement home had threatened to evict her for throwing parties. The home later confirmed the threat, but reached a settlement with Droniak that allowed her to keep partying – but not supply alcoholic drinks.”

item.title: Hallowen 2K26 – Some Old Web 1.0 Horror Fansites
item.description: Brandon’s Journal: “Recently, I took a look back at some old abandoned Scream fansites I found online. I had fun conducting a little internet archaeology and discovering these old works of love before they disappear forever. Sadly, Web 1.0 is dying as the internet continues to grow, and I guess I feel a certain obligation to keep some of that spirit alive. That’s what inspired me to create this post to begin with, and I feel like paying homage to those who came before is only right.”

item.title: On ‘Settle In,’ Kathryn Jezer-Morton and Geoff Bennett discuss social media’s impact
item.description: PBS NewsHour: “Social media lets us share our lives with family, friends, and strangers. But how do people decide what to post, what to leave out, and what do those decisions say about them? On ‘Settle In,’ Geoff Bennett discusses that with Kathryn Jezer-Morton, author of ‘The Story of Your Life,’ a new book about how the incentives of social media platforms have narrowed the kinds of stories we tell.”

item.title: Internet trade group sues California over social media warning labels
item.description: Courthouse News Service: “NetChoice, a trade association whose members include Meta, Google and TikTok, sued California on Thursday to stop a state law requiring social media platforms to display warning labels for users under 18 about the mental health risks of social media use. NetChoice said in a complaint filed in Los Angeles federal court that the law, which goes into effect on Jan. 1, violates the First Amendment prohibition against compelled speech.”

item.title: How a Legal Backlash Against Big Tech Is Forcing Big Changes
item.description: New York Times: “For decades, tech giants grew at breakneck speeds as Congress struggled to keep pace with the consequences of the companies’ rapidly booming businesses. But a new de facto regulatory regime has emerged over the past year as courts clobber the biggest internet companies. And for the first time, their product designs and advertising models — which critics say treat users as products — are costing the companies serious money.”

item.title: Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest
item.description: Ars Technica: “A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries.” Good evening, Internet…
